Mammaprint [4982]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Mamaprint notes

Visuals of a mammogram.

Having a Mammogram can fill the average person with dread. And even though your results might be clear there is always the possibility that at your next mammogram the big C may be an issue you need to face.

The statistics around breats cancer are alarming. Since the 2008 GLOBOCAN (Cancer statistic database) estimates, the incidence of breast cancer has grown by more than 20%, and related mortality has increased by 14%.
Breast cancer is now the common cause of cancer-related death among women (522,000 deaths in 2012), and it is the most frequently diagnosed cancer among women in 140 of 184 countries represented in this database.

And then after the mammogram, if it turns out to be positive what are your options? The traditional course of treatment is typically surgery, followed by an often difficult course of chemotherapy to try to make sure the cancer doesn't recur.

But, a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine in October last year found that about 46% of women who were at high risk of breast cancer recurrence after surgery might not actually need chemotherapy — which often comes with debilitating side effects like profound fatigue, nausea, hair loss, and a weakened immune system.
This was the result of a five-year-long clinical trial of about 6,700 women who had been diagnosed with early-stage breast cancer. Stellenbosch University was part of the study.

The doagnostic test is called "MammaPrint" that screens breast cancer tumors for the activity in 70 genes. The results of the test are designed to give cancer doctors an idea of whether someone is at a low or high genetic risk for recurrence.

The test is FDA approved and costs R 29 000 which is considerably less than the R 150 000 of chemo therapy. The biopsy of the tumour is tested in the Netherlands.

It is not covered by Discovery yet, the will pay for another test called Oncotype DX which is a more expensive test, tests only 21 genes and does not give a definite yes/no answer that the Mammaprint test does.

Dr Maritha Kotze – geneticist part of the Study
Dr Langenhoven – oncologist that uses Mammaprint
Two case studies that have had the test and received positive and negative results.

Press Release:


Mammaprint
Breast cancer is the most common form of cancer among South African women. For some, chemotherapy with its toxic side effects is the only route – but
finding out whether or not you require chemo, is often a guessing game. Now with precision genomic testing, the DNA of cancer cells in the breast tissue can
be analysed. Carte Blanche explores how the Mammaprint test could save some patients with early stage cancer, from having to go through the rigors of
chemotherapy

Script:


STUDIO LINK: Breast cancer is the commonest cancer among South African women and a leading cause of death worldwide. For some, chemotherapy with its toxic side effects is the only route – but finding out whether or not you require chemo is often a guessing game. Not anymore….

Mammaprint Script

V/O
In the trenches of the First World War, mustard gas blistered the lungs and throat of soldiers who inhaled it. War poet Wilfred Owen wrote about men ‘guttering, choking and drowning’…before his helpless sight.

But according to cancer surgeon Dr Ettienne Myburgh, the chemical also had another curious effect:

Ettienne
‘the people that didn’t die from the mustard gas immediately died because their bone marrow stopped producing cells.’


V/O
The significance of this for medical research was not realised until World War II.
Researchers, hoping to develop an antidote in case Germany deployed mustard gas again, speculated that if the compound could destroy healthy cells, it might have an effect on rapidly-dividing cancer cells.

Ettienne
“They saw that they could actually kill those cancer cells in the bone marrow by giving the patients small doses of mustard gas.”

V/O
Which is what modern day chemotherapy does.

V/O
Although it can extend life, chemo’s impact on the body is severe. Ask anyone who has cancer.

Heidi
“What affected me most was my heart, it affects your heart muscles and I was so weak that I could not brush my teeth I couldn’t put my hand up, I couldn’t do anything. Ja, that was tough for me.”

V/O
Heidi Oosthuizen and Juliet Francis were both diagnosed with early stage breast cancer.

Heidi
“I basically felt like a nodule in my breast, but it didn’t worry me so much because I am very prone to having cysts. I went for a mammogram. It looks like a cyst but inside the cyst was a like more dense tissue and that worried them.”

Juliet
“I then had the mammogram and the ultrasound and they picked up a lump. I was devastated it was the last thing I was expecting.”

(Up sound “Going with the compression.”)

Link
Having a mammogram fills many women with dread and those that are tested regularily understand that been given the all clear on one visit might well be followed by a positive tes for cancer on the next.

Juliet
“It’s the three words – you have cancer. It’s the 3 words you dread to hear.”

Heidi
“But I never thought that I would get it.”

V/O
First both Heidi and Juliet had lumpectomies, a surgical operation which involves removing the tumour and surrounding tissue. Then they had to consider Chemo as the next stage of therapy.

Heidi
“If there was any chance that I could pass by chemo I would take it.”

V/O
Oncologist Dr Rika Pienaar says the effects of chemotherapy can be devastating on the body.

“Chemotherapy is very toxic, cardio toxicity, infertility,push you into the menopause, cognitive problems, some women lose their jobs you know.”

V/O
It’s a difficult decision for both doctors and patients.

John
“Do you have a sense before the process unfolds of who will need chemo and who will not?”

Lizanne
“For quite a significant amount of patients we have to rely on our gut feelings as oncologists and that to me is quite daunting. We have studies that show our gut feel is wrong in nearly 50% of cases we call.



V/O
According to Dr Lizanne Langenhoven, this may result in patients undergoing unnecessary chemotherapy.

‘So it means that half the patients might get chemo without benefit, whereas we might be omitting chemo for patients that actually do need to be treated.”

V/O
But what if you knew the genetic make-up of your cancer and could predict whether chemotherapy was the required course of treatment.

You can through Genomics, says Dr Vikash Sewram, Director of the African Cancer Institute in Stellenbosch.

Vikash
“One of the issues around precision medicine is looking at the ability of our genetic profile to predict disease but also to predict outcomes of therapy that we receive and I think if one is able to do so then one is able to decide what treatments may be beneficial to us before actually receiving them.”

V/O
Genomics is changing the way medicine is practiced. There are currently several different tests worldwide looking at the DNA of certain cancer types.

One of these is the Mammaprint. It analyses 70 genes active in the tumours of early stage breast cancer patients and assesses the nature of the disease and directs the most appropriate treatment. This is more accurate than traditional clinical guidelines which rely on indirect features like the size and growth pattern of a cancer.'

Dr Ettienne Myburgh
“We have realised that we were not good at selecting patients accurately, so what we have been doing over the years is including more and more patients to have chemotherapy so that we don’t end up missing someone by chance. With genomics now we can theoretically move in the other direction by saying we can exclude more and more patients from having unnecessary treatment.”

V/O

Clinically breast cancer patients are divided into 3 groups those who are high risk will would get chemo therapy and low risk will not. But about 50% of patients fall inbetween these two and they are the difficult ones to treat.

Because Heidi and Juliet fell into this intermediate group , after removing their tumours, the tissue was biopsied and sent to Mammaprint laboratories in Holland to determine whether chemotherapy would be beneficial.

The Mammaprint trial showed that almost half of this group, didn’t need to go the chemotherapy route.

V/O
Geneticist Prof Maritha Kotze of Stellenbosch University has been compiling a South African genomic database for 9 years. This information is an in valuable resource for scientists studying the disease.

Maritha
“In South Africa we can only say that we spared about half of the patients that we tested. Up to now we have tested more than 300 that is why I said 150 we have spared from chemotherapy.”

V/O
After a few weeks, Juliet received the news she’d been waiting for.

Juliet
“You had the Mammaprint test – what were the results?”

“It came back that I fell into the low risk category. What that basically meant is that I would not benefit from chemo and had we gone on just the ordinary prognostic, indications are that they use the specialist and the oncologist, they actually would have recommended that I have chemo.”


V/O
Not only is there the health benefit of not having chemo but there is also a cost benefit.
The Mammaprint test costs around R 29 000 which is a lot cheaper than chemo at R 150 000.

Although her news wasn’t good, Heidi is glad she knows for sure that chemo is the only route for her.

Heidi
“Dr Myburgh phoned and he said to me unfortunately the test results, it is a high risk cancer, which means that it is aggressive and it will spread fast sorry but you have to have the chemo. And I was fine with that because I knew then it’s the right decision.”

V/O
Breast cancer is on the increase and is the leading cause of cancer deaths amongst women. Dr Pienaar believes that the advances in geneomic medicine will help give her patients the best treatment possible.

Rika
“If I can prevent a chemotherapy perscription, in 50% of patient population that I would normally perscribe it. It is absolutely wonderful and exciting new tool and ally for me in treating my breast cancer patients.”

Lizanne
“The decision we make are heavy as oncologists. I sleep better at night because of this test.”




Promo 10 seconds

Breast cancer is the commonest form of cancer amongst South African women. For some, chemotherapy with its toxic side effects is the only route, but now thanks to genomic testing not all women may need it.

Promo 15 secs

V/O
It’s something most cancer patients try to avoid.
(Should I say breast cancer patients?)
Heidi
“If there was anyway I could pass the chemo route I would take it.”

V/O
But what if you knew the genetic make-up of your cancer and could predict whether chemotherapy was the best course of treatment. Now you can with genomic testing.


Promo 2 15 secs

V/O
It’s called precision medicine and scientists are now able to interpret the behavior of breast cancer tumours by looking at their DNA.
The Mammaprint test analyses 70 genes active in the tumours of early stage breast cancer patients and can save some from having to
go through the rigours of chemotherapy.
